questions.question: What verses support the doctrine of total depravity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:10-12, Eph 2:1-3, Gen 6:5
questions.response:
The doctrine of **Total Depravity** (often the first point of the five points of Calvinism) teaches that as a result of the Fall, every aspect of human nature is corrupted by sin. This does not mean that humans are as "evil" as they possibly could be, but that sin has affected every part of their being—including the mind, will, and emotions—rendering them spiritually dead and incapable of choosing God or saving themselves without divine intervention.

Here are the key Bible verses categorized by how they support this doctrine:

### 1. The Universal Sinfulness of Man
These verses establish that sin is not a rare mistake but a universal condition that affects everyone.

*   **Romans 3:10–12:** "As it is written: 'None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one.'"
    *   *Support:* This passage explicitly denies that anyone naturally seeks after God or does genuine spiritual good.
*   **Romans 3:23:** "For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
*   **1 Kings 8:46:** "...for there is no one who does not sin."
*   **Psalm 14:2–3:** "The Lord looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God. They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one."

### 2. The Corruption of the Heart and Mind
These verses show that sin is not merely external actions but stems from a corrupt internal nature.

*   **Genesis 6:5:** "The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually."
    *   *Support:* This describes the "total" nature of depravity before the flood—every thought and intention was consistently evil.
*   **Genesis 8:21:** "...the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth."
*   **Jeremiah 17:9:** "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"
    *   *Support:* The human heart (the center of will and emotion) is described as sick and deceitful, incapable of curing itself.
*   **Ecclesiastes 9:3:** "Also, the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead."
*   **John 2:24–25:** "But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them... for he himself knew what was in man."

### 3. Spiritual Death and Inability
These verses teach that fallen humans are spiritually "dead," meaning they are unresponsive to God and unable to change their state without being made alive first.

*   **Ephesians 2:1–3:** "And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked... following the course of this world... by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind."
    *   *Support:* Spiritually dead people cannot walk toward God; they follow the world and the flesh. It notes this is our state "by nature."
*   **Ephesians 2:5:** "...even when we were dead in our trespasses, [God] made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved..."
*   **Colossians 2:13:** "And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses."
*   **1 Corinthians 2:14:** "The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned."
    *   *Support:* The "natural" (unregenerated) person lacks the capacity to understand or accept spiritual truth.

### 4. The Bondage of the Will
These verses indicate that apart from God's grace, the human will is in bondage to sin and cannot choose to follow God.

*   **Romans 8:7–8:** "For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God."
    *   *Support:* The inability is emphasized here ("it cannot"). A person set on the flesh is not just unwilling, but unable to submit to God.
*   **John 6:44:** "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day."
    *   *Support:* Jesus states that coming to Him is impossible for a person unless the Father acts first ("draws him").
*   **John 6:65:** "And he said, 'This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.'"
*   **John 8:34:** "Jesus answered them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.'"
    *   *Support:* A slave does not have the freedom to simply leave their master; they are in bondage.
*   **Romans 6:16:** "Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey...?"
*   **2 Timothy 2:25–26:** "...God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will."
    *   *Support:* Repentance is described as something that must be *granted* by God, implying we cannot generate it on our own while under the enemy's capture.

### 5. The Inability to Produce Righteousness
These verses emphasize that even our "good" acts are tainted by sin if not done from a heart of faith and regeneration.

*   **Isaiah 64:6:** "We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment..."
*   **Hebrews 11:6:** "And without faith it is impossible to please him..."
    *   *Support:* Since the unregenerate person lacks faith (as a gift of God), they cannot please God in any way.

questions.question: Which passages teach justification by faith alone?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:28, Eph 2:8-9, Gal 2:16
questions.response:
The doctrine of **justification by faith alone** (often called *Sola Fide*) teaches that a person is declared righteous (justified) before God solely through faith in Jesus Christ, rather than through good works or adherence to the law.

While the exact phrase "faith alone" appears only once in the New Testament (in a slightly different context in James 2:24), the concept is pervasive throughout the writings of Paul, John, and the other apostles.

Here are the primary passages that teach this doctrine:

### 1. Romans 3:28 (The Explicit Statement)
This is perhaps the clearest verse in the Bible articulating the specific mechanism of justification.
> "For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law."

### 2. Galatians 2:16 (The Contrast)
Paul emphasizes here that even the "works" required by the Mosaic law cannot save; only faith in Christ can.
> "yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified."

### 3. Ephesians 2:8-9 (Grace and Faith)
This passage establishes that salvation (and by extension, justification) is a gift of grace, not a reward for human effort.
> "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast."

### 4. Romans 4:5 (Faith vs. Merit)
Here, Paul explains that faith is not a "work" that earns wages; it is simply trusting God.
> "And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness."

### 5. Romans 5:1 (The Result)
Paul describes the peace that comes from this specific transaction.
> "Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."

### 6. Philippians 3:9 (Righteousness from God)
Paul contrasts his own attempts at righteousness through the law with the superior righteousness that comes through faith.
> "and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith."

### 7. Galatians 3:24-25 (The Role of the Law)
Paul argues that the Law was meant to show us our need for Christ, not to save us.
> "So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian."

### 8. John 5:24 (Jesus’ Teaching)
Jesus Himself teaches that the act of believing results in the transition from death to life (justification).
> "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life."

### 9. Acts 13:38-39 (Early Church Preaching)
In one of the first major sermons recorded in the early church, Paul declares freedom from the law through Jesus.
> "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."

### 10. Old Testament Foundation: Genesis 15:6
The New Testament writers often look back to Abraham as the prototype of justification by faith. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6.
> "And he believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness."

### Summary
The consistent biblical witness is that justification is a legal verdict rendered by God in which the sinner is declared righteous. This verdict is based on the finished work of Christ (His life, death, and resurrection) and is received by the individual through faith alone, apart from any personal merit or good deeds.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach the doctrine of original sin?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 5:12, Rom 5:18-19, Ps 51:5, Gen 3:6-7
questions.response:
The doctrine of original sin—the belief that humanity has inherited a sinful nature and a state of alienation from God due to the disobedience of Adam and Eve—is primarily derived from specific passages in the Old and New Testaments.

Here are the key Scripture passages traditionally cited to teach this doctrine, categorized by their specific contribution to the theology.

### 1. The Historical Fall (Genesis 3)
While the term "original sin" is not found in the text, the narrative of the Fall provides the foundation for the doctrine. It describes the entrance of sin, corruption, and death into the human experience.
*   **Genesis 3:** The account of Adam and Eve eating the forbidden fruit.
*   **Genesis 3:6-7:** "So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate. Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths." (This illustrates immediate shame and a broken relationship with God).

### 2. The Inherited Nature (Psalm 51 and Job)
These passages indicate that sinfulness is not just something we *do*, but something we *are* from the very beginning of our existence.
*   **Psalm 51:5:** "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me." (David acknowledges that his sin nature goes back to his conception).
*   **Job 14:4:** "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one." (Suggests that a sinful parent cannot produce a morally pure child).
*   **Job 15:14:** "What is man, that he can be pure? Or he who is born of a woman, that he can be righteous?"

### 3. Universal Sinfulness (Romans 3 and Others)
These passages argue that because Adam sinned, *every* human being is born with a sinful nature and inevitably commits sin.
*   **Romans 3:9-12, 23:** "What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all; for we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin... 'None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one.' ... for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
*   **1 Kings 8:46:** "...for there is no one who does not sin."
*   **Psalm 14:2-3:** "The Lord looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God. They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one."

### 4. The Federal Headship of Adam (Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15)
These are the most theologically dense passages regarding original sin. They explain *how* Adam’s sin affects the rest of humanity. The concept is often called "Federal Headship," meaning Adam acted as the representative of the human race.
*   **Romans 5:12, 15-19:** "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned... But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many... For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ. Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous."
*   **1 Corinthians 15:21-22:** "For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive."

### 5. The State of the Unregenerate (Ephesians 2)
This passage describes the spiritual state of a person before they are saved, characterizing them as naturally rebellious.
*   **Ephesians 2:1-3:** "And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience—among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind." (The phrase "by nature children of wrath" strongly implies an inherited sinful status).

### 6. The Depravity of the Heart (Jeremiah and Genesis)
These passages describe the internal corruption of human nature that stems from the Fall.
*   **Jeremiah 17:9:** "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"
*   **Genesis 6:5:** "The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually."
*   **Genesis 8:21:** "...the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth."

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of the Trinity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14, John 1:1, Gen 1:26
questions.response:
The word "Trinity" does not appear in the Bible. However, Christian theologians and biblical scholars argue that the doctrine is a "necessary deduction" from the entirety of Scripture. The teaching is derived from synthesizing three key biblical truths:

1.  **There is only one God.** (Monotheism)
2.  **The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God.** (Deity)
3.  **The Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct persons.** (Distinction)

Here is a breakdown of where the Bible teaches these specific components, which together form the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity.

### 1. The Bible Teaches There is Only One God (Monotheism)
The doctrine of the Trinity begins with the affirmation of strict monotheism found in the Old Testament and reaffirmed in the New Testament.

*   **Deuteronomy 6:4:** "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one."
*   **Isaiah 45:5:** "I am the Lord, and there is no other; besides me there is no God."
*   **James 2:19:** "You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!"
*   **1 Timothy 2:5:** "For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."

### 2. The Bible Teaches the Deity of the Father, Son, and Spirit
While there is only one God, Scripture attributes the attributes of deity to three distinct persons.

**The Father is God:**
*   **1 Corinthians 8:6:** "Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist."

**The Son (Jesus) is God:**
*   **John 1:1:** "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." (This establishes that the Word [Jesus] is distinct from the Father yet shares the same divine nature).
*   **John 20:28:** Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"
*   **Colossians 2:9:** "For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily."
*   **Titus 2:13:** "...waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."
*   **Hebrews 1:8:** But of the Son he says, "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever..."

**The Holy Spirit is God:**
*   **Acts 5:3-4:** Peter accuses Ananias of lying to the Holy Spirit, then adds, "You have not lied to man but to God." This equates the Spirit with God.
*   **1 Corinthians 3:16:** "Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?"
*   **Hebrews 9:14:** Refers to the "eternal Spirit," implying an attribute (eternity) belonging only to God.

### 3. The Bible Teaches The Three are Distinct Persons
The Bible distinguishes the three persons so that they are not merely different names or modes of the same person (a heresy known as Modalism). They interact with one another and exist simultaneously

questions.question: What passages affirm the full deity of Jesus Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: John 1:1, John 1:14, Col 2:9, Heb 1:3, Phil 2:6
questions.response:
The doctrine of the full deity of Jesus Christ is central to Christian theology and is supported by numerous passages throughout the New Testament. These passages generally fall into categories: explicit statements of His divinity, attributions of divine names (Yahweh), descriptions of His role in creation, and the attribution of divine prerogatives (such as forgiving sins).

Here are the primary biblical passages that affirm the full deity of Jesus Christ:

### 1. Explicit Statements of Divinity
These verses directly identify Jesus as God.

*   **John 1:1:** "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
    *   *Context:* This establishes the eternal nature of the Word (Jesus) and clearly states His divine nature.
*   **John 1:14:** "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
    *   *Context:* This bridges the divinity of verse 1 with the humanity of Jesus.
*   **John 20:28:** "Thomas answered him, 'My Lord and my God!'"
    *   *Context:* After the resurrection, Thomas addresses Jesus directly with the Greek titles *Kyrios* (Lord) and *Theos* (God). Jesus accepts this worship rather than correcting it.
*   **Titus 2:13:** "...waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."
    *   *Context:* Paul explicitly refers to Jesus as "our great God and Savior."
*   **Hebrews 1:8:** "But of the Son he says, 'Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.'"
    *   *Context:* God the Father is speaking to the Son and addresses Him as "God."
*   **2 Peter 1:1:** "...Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ. To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ."
    *   *Context:* Peter uses a grammatical structure that identifies Jesus as both God and Savior.
*   **Romans 9:5:** "...To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen."

### 2. The "I AM" Statements
In the Old Testament, the name of God (Yahweh) is related to the phrase "I AM" (Exodus 3:14). Jesus applies this title to Himself, asserting His eternality and identity with the God of the Old Testament.

*   **John 8:58:** "Jesus said to them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.'"
    *   *Context:* The immediate reaction of the Jewish leaders was to pick up stones to kill Him for blasphemy, understanding that He was claiming to be the eternal God.
*   **John 18:5-6:** When Jesus identified Himself to the soldiers saying "I am," the text notes, "they drew back and fell to the ground."
    *   *Context:* This suggests the divine authority and power inherent in His presence and name.

### 3. The Creator and Sustainer
The Bible teaches that God alone created the universe. Several passages attribute this work to Jesus.

*   **John 1:3:** "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made."
*   **Colossians 1:16-17:** "For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together."
*   **Hebrews 1:2:** "...but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world."

### 4. Equality with God the Father
These passages emphasize that Jesus shares the same essence, glory, and authority as the Father.

*   **Philippians 2:6-7:** "...who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men."
    *   *Context:* Paul states that Jesus pre-existed in the "form of God" and possessed "equality with God."
*   **John 10:30:** "I and the Father are one."
    *   *Context:* Again, the Jews understood this as a claim to deity, stating, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God" (John 10:33).
*   **Colossians 2:9:** "For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily."

### 5. Divine Attributes and Prerogatives
Jesus is described as possessing attributes that belong only to God (omniscience, omnipresence, eternality) and performing actions only God can perform (forgiving sins, receiving worship).

*   **Matthew 9:2-6 (and Mark 2:5-7):** Jesus forgives the sins of a paralytic. The scribes object, thinking, "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" Jesus heals the man to prove He has the authority to forgive sins.
*   **John 21:17:** Peter confesses to Jesus, "Lord, you know everything." Jesus accepts this confession of omniscience.
*   **Matthew 28:18:** "And Jesus came and said to them, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.'"
*   **Hebrews 13:8:** "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever." (Immutability/Eternality).
*   **Revelation 1:17-18:** Jesus refers to Himself as "the First and the Last" and "the living one" who died and is alive forevermore—titles claimed by Yahweh in Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12.

### 6. Old Testament Prophecies Applied to Jesus
The New Testament writers apply Old Testament verses specifically about Yahweh (God) to Jesus.

*   **Isaiah 40:3 vs. Matthew 3:3:** Isaiah says, "Prepare the way of the LORD [Yahweh]." The Gospels apply this to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus.
*   **Joel 2:32 vs. Romans 10:13:** Joel says, "Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD [Yahweh] will be saved." Paul applies this to calling on the name of Jesus.
*   **Psalm 102:25-27 vs. Hebrews 1:10-12:** The Psalmist addresses God as the Creator who laid the foundation of the earth. Hebrews applies this directly to the Son.

questions.question: Which Bible passages teach the bodily resurrection of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 15:3-8, Matt 28:5-6, Luke 24:39, John 20:27
questions.response:
The bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ is the central tenet of the Christian faith and is affirmed throughout the New Testament. The Bible emphasizes not just that Jesus’ spirit survived, but that His physical body was raised from the dead, transformed, and glorified.

Here are the key Bible passages categorized by how they teach the bodily resurrection.

### 1. The Gospel Narratives (The Physical Evidence)
The Gospels provide the most direct evidence of a physical resurrection. They describe Jesus interacting with the physical world—eating, touching, and being touched—after His death.

*   **Luke 24:36–43:** This is perhaps the most explicit passage regarding the physical nature of the resurrection. The disciples, terrified, think they are seeing a ghost. Jesus responds:
    > *"Look at my hands and my feet. It is I myself! Touch me and see; a ghost does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have."* ... *"He said to them, 'Have you anything here to eat?' They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate it in their presence."*
*   **John 20:24–29:** The account of "Doubting Thomas." Jesus invites Thomas to physically touch His wounds.
    > *"Then he said to Thomas, 'Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.'"*
*   **John 20:17:** Jesus tells Mary Magdalene, *"Do not hold on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father."* This implies He could be physically held and touched.
*   **Matthew 28:9:** The women clasped his feet and worshiped him. You cannot clasp the feet of a spirit.

### 2. The Empty Tomb (The Absence of the Body)
The resurrection accounts emphasize that the body was gone, not just that Jesus appeared as a vision. The physical absence of the body in the tomb necessitates a physical explanation.

*   **Luke 24:2–3:** *"They found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they entered, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus."*
*   **John 20:6–7:** Peter and the other disciple enter the tomb and see the linen wrappings lying there. The fact that the grave clothes were left behind suggests the body passed through them (or was unwrapped) rather than the body being stolen (which would likely have involved taking the body wrapped in the linens).

### 3. Paul’s Theology (The Nature of the Resurrected Body)
The Apostle Paul addresses the bodily resurrection directly, specifically countering the idea that resurrection is only spiritual.

*   **1 Corinthians 15:3–8:** Paul passes on the early creed of the church, emphasizing that Jesus appeared to specific individuals (Cephas, the twelve, the five hundred, James, and finally Paul).
*   **1 Corinthians 15:12–19:** Paul argues that if there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised. He links Christ's resurrection directly to the future resurrection of believers.
*   **1 Corinthians 15:35–44:** Paul explains the nature of the resurrected body. He distinguishes between the "natural body" (perishable) and the "spiritual body" (imperishable). However, he uses the analogy of a seed. A seed is planted "physical" but raised "spiritual." It is a transformation of matter, not a discarding of matter.
    > *"So will it be with the resurrection of the dead. The body that is sown is perishable, it is raised imperishable; it is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power."*
*   **Philippians 3:21:** Paul states that Jesus *"will transform our lowly bodies so that they will be like his glorious body."* This implies our future bodies will be physical like His current resurrected body.

### 4. The Early Church Proclamation (Acts)
In the book of Acts, the apostles consistently preached that the resurrection was a physical, historical event involving a body.

*

questions.question: What Scripture supports the doctrine of substitutionary atonement?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Isa 53:5-6, 2 Cor 5:21, 1 Pet 2:24, Rom 3:25
questions.response:
The doctrine of substitutionary atonement teaches that Jesus Christ died in the place of sinners, taking the punishment they deserved to satisfy the justice and wrath of God. This is often summarized by the phrase "He died for us."

Here are the primary Scripture passages that support this doctrine, categorized by the type of evidence they provide.

### 1. The Suffering Servant (Isaiah 53)
This Old Testament prophecy is considered the clearest foreshadowing of substitutionary atonement in the entire Bible.

*   **Isaiah 53:4-6:** "Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows... But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed. We all, like sheep, have gone astray... and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all."
*   **Isaiah 53:12:** "Because he poured out his life unto death, and was numbered with the transgressors. For he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors."

### 2. The "Ransom" and "Service" of Jesus (Gospels)
Jesus explicitly stated that His life would be given as a ransom for others.

*   **Mark 10:45:** "For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
*   **Matthew 20:28:** (Parallel to Mark 10:45) "...to give his life as a ransom for many."
*   **John 10:11:** "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep."
*   **John 11:50-52:** (Caiaphas prophesying) "It is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish... not only for that nation but also for the scattered children of God, to bring them together and make them one."

### 3. The "Great Exchange" (Paul’s Epistles)
The Apostle Paul provides the most detailed theological explanation of substitution, often describing it as an exchange where Christ takes our sin and we receive His righteousness.

*   **2 Corinthians 5:21:** "God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God."
*   **Galatians 1:4:** "[Jesus] gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father."
*   **Galatians 3:13:** "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written: 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a pole.'"
*   **Romans 5:6-8:** "You see, at just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly... God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us."

### 4. Bearing Sin and the Curse (General Epistles)
The authors of the other epistles emphasize that Jesus physically bore the penalty of sin in His body.

*   **1 Peter 2:24:** "He himself bore our sins in his body on the cross, so that we might die to sins and live for righteousness; by his wounds you have been healed."
*   **1 Peter 3:18:** "For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God."
*   **Hebrews 9:28:** "So Christ was sacrificed once to take away the sins of many; and he will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who are waiting for him."

### 5. Propitiation (Turning Away Wrath)
Several passages use the specific Greek word *hilasterion* (propitiation), meaning that Jesus’s death was a sacrifice that appeased or satisfied God’s righteous anger against sin.

*   **Romans 3:25:** "God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement [propitiation], through the shedding of his blood—to be received by faith."
*   **1 John 2:2:** "He is the atoning sacrifice [propitiation] for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world."
*   **1 John 4:10:** "This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice [propitiation] for our sins."

### Summary
The consistent narrative of Scripture is that sin separates humanity from a holy God and incurs a debt of death (Romans 6:23). Substitutionary atonement is the biblical solution: Jesus steps into that gap, dies the death we deserve, and credits us with His righteousness so that we can be reconciled to God.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the imputation of Christ's righteousness?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 2 Cor 5:21, Rom 4:3-6, Phil 3:9, Rom 5:19
questions.response:
The doctrine of the **imputation of Christ's righteousness** teaches that when a person has faith in Christ, Christ’s perfect obedience and righteousness are credited ("imputed") to their account. Consequently, God views the believer as perfectly righteous, not because of their own deeds, but because of Christ’s.

While the specific phrase "imputation of Christ’s righteousness" does not appear verbatim in the Bible, the concept is taught explicitly through several key theological terms and metaphors, primarily the Greek word *logizomai* (to reckon, count, or impute).

Here are the primary passages where this doctrine is taught:

### 1. 2 Corinthians 5:21 (The Great Exchange)
This is perhaps the most direct and explicit statement regarding the exchange of our sin for Christ's righteousness.

> "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God."

*   **The Teaching:** This verse describes a double imputation. Our sin was imputed to Christ on the cross ("he made him to be sin"), and His righteousness is imputed to us ("we might become the righteousness of God"). Paul clarifies that this righteousness is not inherent to us but is found "in him" (in Christ).

### 2. Romans 4:5–8 (Imputation, Not Infusion)
In Romans 4, Paul uses the example of Abraham to prove that justification is by faith alone. He focuses on the word *logizomai* (counted/reckoned).

> "And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness... just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: 'Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.'"

*   **The Teaching:** God counts the believer as righteous **apart from works**. If righteousness were something we achieved internally (infused righteousness), it would not be a matter of "counting" or "reckoning" but of measuring. The fact that God "counts" a sinner as righteous implies that the righteousness is credited to their account from an outside source—namely, Christ.

### 3. Romans 5:17–19 (The Adam/Christ Contrast)
Paul parallels Adam and Christ to explain how salvation works. Just as Adam’s sin was imputed to all humanity (because we were "in" him), Christ’s obedience is imputed to all who are "in" Him.

> "For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ. Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous."

*   **The Teaching:** Paul argues that we are made righteous by Christ's "obedience." This refers to His entire life of active obedience to the Father, culminating in the cross. This righteousness is a "free gift" received by grace, contrasting with the condemnation we inherited from Adam.

### 4. Philippians 3:8–9 (A Foreign Righteousness)
Paul describes his own religious background as worthless in comparison to the righteousness he gains through Christ.

> "...and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith."

*   **The Teaching:** Paul explicitly distinguishes between two types of righteousness: "my own" (inherent, achieved by keeping the law) and "that which comes through faith" (imputed, coming from God). The righteousness that just

questions.question: What passages describe the process of sanctification?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Thess 4:3, Phil 2:12-13, 2 Cor 3:18, Heb 12:14
questions.response:
Sanctification is the process of being set apart for God’s purposes and progressively becoming more like Jesus Christ. Unlike justification (which is a one-time legal declaration of righteousness), sanctification is a continuous work of God’s grace that involves the believer's active participation.

Here are key biblical passages that describe this process, categorized by the specific aspect of sanctification they highlight.

### 1. The Cooperative Nature (God’s Work and Our Effort)
These passages emphasize that while God provides the power, the believer must actively engage in the process.

*   **Philippians 2:12–13**
    > "Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure."
    *   **The Process:** This is perhaps the clearest description of the "synergy" of sanctification. We are to "work out" (active effort) what God is "working in" (divine power). It describes a life of active obedience relying on God's inner enablement.

*   **1 Timothy 4:7**
    > "Rather train yourself for godliness; for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come."
    *   **The Process:** Paul uses the metaphor of athletic training. Sanctification requires discipline, practice, and repetitive effort to become "godly."

### 2. Transformation and Renewal
These passages focus on the internal change—how the mind and heart are reshaped over time.

*   **Romans 12:2**
    > "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect."
    *   **The Process:** Sanctification happens through the "renewal of the mind." As we fill our minds with God’s truth, our way of thinking changes, which in turn changes our behavior.

*   **2 Corinthians 3:18**
    > "And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit."
    *   **The Process:** This describes sanctification as a metamorphosis ("transformed"). It is a progressive movement "from one degree of glory to another," implying it is a journey, not a destination reached in this life. The mechanism is "beholding" (focusing on Christ).

### 3. Putting Off and Putting On
These passages describe the practical daily reality of sanctification: removing sinful habits and adopting righteous ones.

*   **Ephesians 4:22–24**
    > "...to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires, and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness."
    *   **The Process:** This uses the metaphor of changing clothes. It is a daily routine of discarding the "old self" (sin patterns) and "putting on" the "new self" (Christlike character).

*   **Colossians 3:5–10**
    > "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you... Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience..."
    *   **The Process:** This intensifies the language to "put to death," suggesting a radical and aggressive stance against sin, replacing it with positive virtues.

### 4. The Role of Suffering and Discipline
These passages explain that trials and difficulties are tools God uses to refine character.

*   **Hebrews 12:10–11**
    > "For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it."
    *   **The Process:** God uses "discipline" (often through trials) not to punish, but to train us so that we may "share his holiness." The process is often painful ("yields the peaceful fruit") but results in righteousness.

*   **James 1:2–4**
    > "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing."
    *   **The Process:** Trials test faith, which produces steadfastness (endurance). Allowing steadfastness to have its "full effect" is the process of moving toward maturity ("perfect and complete").

### 5. The Role of the Spirit and the Word
These passages highlight the means by which the process occurs.

*   **John 17:17**
    > "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth."
    *   **The Process:** Jesus prays that the Father would sanctify believers. The instrument of this sanctification is "the truth" (Scripture). The Word of God acts as a cleansing agent.

*   **1 Peter 2:2**
    > "Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation."
    *   **The Process:** Just as a baby grows by craving milk, believers grow (sanctify) by craving and consuming the Word of God.

### 6. The Tension: "Already" but "Not Yet"
These passages acknowledge that while we are positionally holy, we are still in the process of becoming practically holy.

*   **Hebrews 10:14**
    > "For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified."
    *   **The Process:** This verse captures the unique tension of the Christian life. We *have been perfected* (legal standing before God) but we are currently *being sanctified* (ongoing reality in daily life).

*   **1 John 3:2–3**
    > "Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure."
    *   **The Process:** The hope of future transformation ("we shall be like him") fuels the present process of purification ("purifies himself"). The future hope drives present obedience.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the means of grace?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 10:17, Acts 2:42, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 28:19
questions.response:
The phrase "means of grace" is theological shorthand rather than a specific phrase found in the Bible. However, the concept is thoroughly biblical. It refers to the ordinary instruments or channels (means) God uses to convey the grace of the Holy Spirit to believers, fostering faith, sanctification, and perseverance.

Historically, Protestant theology (particularly in Reformed and Lutheran traditions) has categorized these means specifically as **Word** (Scripture) and **Sacraments** (Baptism and the Lord’s Supper). Some traditions, such as Methodism, also include **Prayer** as a means of grace.

Here is where Scripture teaches about each of these means.

### 1. The Word of God (Scripture)
The Bible teaches that the Word is not merely information, but a vehicle through which God creates faith and sustains spiritual life.

*   **Romans 10:17:** "So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ."
*   **1 Peter 1:23:** "...since you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God."
*   **2 Timothy 3:16–17:** "All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work."
*   **John 17:17:** "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth."

### 2. Baptism
Scripture presents baptism not just as a symbol of the believer's choice, but as an act of God where He delivers forgiveness, the Holy Spirit, and union with Christ.

*   **Acts 2:38:** "And Peter said to them, 'Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'"
*   **Titus 3:5:** "He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit."
*   **Romans 6:3–4:** "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life."
*   **1 Peter 3:21:** "Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ."

*   **1 Corinthians 10:16:** "The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood

questions.question: What Bible passages support covenant theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 17:7, Jer 31:31-34, Heb 8:6-13, Gal 3:29
questions.response:
Covenant Theology is a framework for interpreting the Bible that understands God's relationship with humanity primarily through the lens of covenants. It emphasizes the continuity between the Old and New Testaments, arguing that there is one people of God (the Church) saved by one covenant of grace, administered differently throughout history.

Here are the key Bible passages that form the scriptural foundation for Covenant Theology, categorized by the theological concepts they support.

### 1. The Covenant of Works (The Adamic Administration)
Covenant Theology posits that God entered into a works-based arrangement with Adam in the Garden. If Adam obeyed, he would earn eternal life; if he disobeyed, he would die.

*   **Hosea 6:7:** *"But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me."*
    *   **Significance:** This is the most direct textual evidence for a covenant with Adam. The prophet compares Israel’s rebellion to Adam’s violation of a covenant.
*   **Romans 5:12–21:** *"Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin... death reigned from Adam to Moses..."*
    *   **Significance:** Paul draws a direct parallel between Adam and Christ. Adam is the "head" or representative of humanity, just as Christ is the head of the Church. This federal (representative) headship is the structural basis for the Covenant of Works.
*   **Galatians 4:4–5:** *"But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law..."*
    *   **Significance:** Christ is seen as the Second Adam who perfectly fulfilled the covenant obligations that the first Adam failed to keep.

### 2. The Covenant of Grace (The Promise of Salvation)
Following the Fall, Covenant Theology sees God initiating a single "Covenant of Grace"—His promise to save sinners by grace through faith, which is revealed progressively throughout Scripture.

*   **Genesis 3:15:** *"I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he shall crush your head, and you shall bruise his heel."*
    *   **Significance:** Often called the *Protoevangelium* (first gospel), this is seen as the first inkling of the Covenant of Grace, where God promises a Savior (the seed of the woman) to defeat the Serpent.
*   **Genesis 17:7:** *"And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you."*
    *   **Significance:** The Abrahamic Covenant is central to Covenant Theology. It establishes that the relationship is based on God's promise ("everlasting covenant") rather than human performance,

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the Lord's Supper?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 26:26-28, Luke 22:19-20
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about the Lord’s Supper (also known as Communion or the Eucharist) in several key passages. These passages are divided into the historical account of its institution, the early church’s practice, and theological instructions.

Here are the primary biblical locations where this is taught:

### 1. The Institution (The Gospels)
The Lord's Supper was instituted by Jesus on the night He was betrayed. The "Synoptic Gospels" (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) provide the narrative account.

*   **Matthew 26:26–29:** While they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, “Take and eat; this is my body.” Then he took a cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you. This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins."
*   **Mark 14:22–25:** A parallel account to Matthew, emphasizing the "blood of the covenant."
*   **Luke 22:14–23:** This account includes the command to "do this in remembrance of me." It also mentions that Jesus will not drink of the fruit of the vine again until the kingdom of God comes.

### 2. The Theological Foundation (The Gospel of John)
While John does not narrate the breaking of the bread and drinking of the wine at the Last Supper (he focuses on the foot washing), he provides the deep theological background for the practice in the "Bread of Life" discourse.

*   **John 6:22–59:** Jesus declares, "I am the bread of life." He specifically says, "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in them" (v. 56). This passage explains the spiritual nourishment and necessity of partaking in Christ.

### 3. The Instruction and Correction (1 Corinthians)
The Apostle Paul provides the most detailed theological instruction regarding the Lord's Supper. He addresses how it should be conducted and the heart attitude required.

*   **1 Corinthians 10:14–17:** Paul teaches about the participation (koinonia) in the body and blood of Christ. He explains that because there is one bread, we, who are many, are one body.
*   **1 Corinthians 11:17–34:** This is the crucial passage for the proper observance of the Supper. Paul:
    *   Repeats the words of institution ("This is my body... this is my blood").
    *   Emphasizes that it is a proclamation of the Lord’s death "until he comes."
    *   Warns against eating in an "unworthy manner" (recognizing the body of the Lord).
    *   Encourages self-examination before partaking.

### 4. The Practice of the Early Church (Acts)
The book of Acts shows how the first Christians immediately began to observe this ordinance.

*   **Acts 2:42:** Describes the early church devoting themselves to the "apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer."
*   **Acts 20:7:** Shows the pattern of the early church gathering "on the first day of the week" specifically "to break bread."

### Summary of Key Teachings from These Passages:
*   **Remembrance:** It is a memorial of Christ's death (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor 11:24).
*   **Participation:** It is a means of sharing in the body and blood of Christ (1 Cor 10:16).
*   **Proclamation:** It declares the Lord's death until He returns (1 Cor 11:26).
*   **Unity:** It represents the unity of the church as one body (1 Cor 10:17).
*   **Self-Examination:** It requires participants to examine their hearts and repent of sin (1 Cor 11:28).

questions.question: What passages address the doctrine of baptism?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4, Col 2:11-12
questions.response:
The doctrine of baptism is addressed extensively throughout the New Testament. The passages generally cover the command to be baptized, the theological meaning of the act, the method used, and its role in salvation.

Here is a categorized list of key passages addressing the doctrine of baptism:

### 1. The Institution and Command of Baptism
These passages establish baptism as a commandment for believers and an initiation into the Christian faith.

*   **The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20):**
    > "Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you."
*   **Mark 16:16:**
    > "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned."
*   **John 3:5:**
    > "Jesus answered, 'Very truly I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless they are born of water and the Spirit.'" (Often interpreted as referring to baptism).

### 2. The Baptism of Jesus
These passages describe Jesus’ own baptism, which serves as a model for Christian baptism and the affirmation of His ministry.

*   **Matthew 3:13–17:** Describes Jesus coming to John the Baptist, the Spirit descending like a dove, and the voice from heaven saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."
*   **Mark 1:9–11:** A parallel account of the event.

### 3. Baptism in the Early Church (The Book of Acts)
Acts provides the narrative history of how the apostles and the early church understood and practiced baptism. It consistently shows baptism following closely after conversion and repentance.

*   **Pentecost (Acts 2:38, 41):**
    > "Peter replied, 'Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.' ... Those who accepted his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to their number that day."
*   **The Ethiopian Eunuch (Acts 8:36–38):**
    > "As they traveled along the road, they came to some water and the eunuch said, 'Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?' ... Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water and Philip baptized him."
*   **Paul’s Conversion (Acts 9:18; Acts 22:16):**
    > "Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized." / "And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized and wash your sins away, calling on his name."
*   **Cornelius (The First Gentiles) (Acts 10:47–48):**
    > "Surely no one can stand in the way of their being baptized with water. They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have. So he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ."
*   **The Philippian Jailer (Acts 16:33):**
    > "At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds; then immediately he and all his household were baptized."
*   **The Corinthians (Acts 18:8):**
    > "Many of the Corinthians who believed Paul and were baptized."

### 4. The Theological Significance of Baptism
The Epistles (letters) explain the spiritual meaning behind the physical act, focusing on union with Christ in His death and resurrection.

*   **Romans 6:3–4 (Union with Christ's Death and Resurrection):**
    > "Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life."
*   **Galatians 3:26–27 (Clothed with Christ):**
    > "So in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith, for all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ."
*   **Colossians 2:11–12 (Circumcision of Christ):**
    > "Having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through your faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead."
*   **1 Peter 3:21 (Baptism as a Pledge):**
    > "...and this water symbolizes baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God. It saves you by the resurrection of Jesus Christ."

### 5. Baptism and the Holy Spirit
These passages distinguish between water baptism and the baptism of the Holy Spirit, or link them together.

*   **1 Corinthians 12:13:**
    > "For we were all baptized by one Spirit so as to form one body—whether Jews or Gentiles, slave or free—and we were all given the one Spirit to drink."
*   **Acts 1:5:**
    > "For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit."

### 6. The Nature of the "One Baptism"
*   **Ephesians 4:4–5:**
    > "There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; one Lord, one faith, one baptism."

### Summary of Doctrinal Views
Different Christian traditions interpret these passages differently:
*   **Mode:** Some insist on full *immersion* (based on Romans 6 "buried" and Acts 8 "went down into the water"), while others practice *affusion* (pouring) or *aspersion* (sprinkling).
*   **Recipients:** Some practice *believer's baptism* (based on accounts of belief preceding baptism in Acts), while others practice *infant baptism* (based on household baptisms like Acts 16:33 and parallels with circumcision).
*   **Efficacy:** Some view it as a necessary *sacrament* for regeneration (ex opere operato), while others view it as an *ordinance* or symbol of obedience and public testimony.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about church government and eldership?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Tim 3:1-7, Titus 1:5-9, Acts 14:23, 1 Pet 5:1-4
questions.response:
While the Bible does not contain a single "Book of Church Government," it provides a robust framework for leadership and church structure throughout the New Testament. The teachings are found primarily in the Pauline Epistles, the book of Acts, and the General Epistles (Peter, James, and John).

Here is a breakdown of where Scripture teaches about church government and eldership, categorized by key themes.

### 1. The Identity and Terminology of Elders
Scripture uses three primary terms interchangeably for the same church office. This establishes the biblical basis for a plurality of leaders.

*   **Acts 20:17, 28:** Paul calls the "elders" (*presbyteros*) of the church in Ephesus, then tells them the Holy Spirit has made them "overseers" (*episkopos*). This proves the terms refer to the same office.
*   **1 Peter 5:1-2:** Peter instructs the "elders" to "shepherd" (*poimen*—the root word for pastor) the flock of God that is among them, exercising oversight.
*   **Titus 1:5-7:** Paul tells Titus to appoint "elders" in every town, then immediately describes them as "overseers" who must hold firm to the trustworthy word.

### 2. The Appointment of Elders
The New Testament shows that elders were not self-appointed but recognized and appointed by apostolic authority or other leaders.

*   **Acts 14:23:** "And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed."
*   **Titus 1:5:** "This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you."

### 3. Qualifications for Elders
The most explicit instructions regarding the character requirements for church leaders are found in the Pastoral Epistles.

*   **1 Timothy 3:1-7:** Paul lists the qualifications for an "overseer" (bishop/elder). The list focuses heavily on character (sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable) and family management (managing his own household well), rather than specific spiritual gifts or business skills.
*   **Titus 1:6-9:** A parallel passage to 1 Timothy 3, adding a specific emphasis on doctrinal soundness: "He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it."

### 4. The Function and Duties of Elders

questions.question: What Bible passages teach about the second coming of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Acts 1:11, 1 Thess 4:16-17, Matt 24:30, Rev 1:7
questions.response:
The Second Coming of Christ (often referred to in the New Testament as the *Parousia*, meaning "arrival" or "presence") is one of the most prominent themes in the Bible. It is estimated that one out of every 25 verses in the New Testament refers to this event. 

Rather than a single passage, the Bible builds its teaching on the Second Coming through various passages that highlight different aspects of the event. Here are the key passages, organized by the themes they teach:

### 1. The Promise and Manner of His Return
These passages establish that Jesus will physically return and describe *how* it will happen.

*   **Acts 1:9-11 (The Ascension):** After Jesus ascends to heaven, two angels tell the disciples, *"Men of Galilee, why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen him go into heaven."* This establishes the return as physical, visible, and personal.
*   **Matthew 24:27, 30:** *"For as lightning that comes from the east is visible even in the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man... Then will appear the sign of the Son of Man in heaven. And then all the peoples of the earth will mourn when they see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven, with power and great glory."* Jesus teaches that His return will be sudden, unmistakable, and globally visible.
*   **Revelation 1:7:** *"Look, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him; and all peoples on earth will mourn because of him."* This echoes Daniel 7 and Matthew 24, emphasizing the universal visibility and the realization of those who rejected Him.

### 2. The Resurrection and Gathering of Believers
Several passages focus on what the Second Coming means for the church—namely, the resurrection of the dead and the uniting of believers with Christ.

*   **1 Thessalonians 4:13-18:** This is perhaps the most detailed passage on the gathering of the church. *"For the Lord himself will come down from heaven, with a loud command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet call of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first. After that, we who are still alive and are left will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will be with the Lord forever."*
*   **1 Corinthians 15:51-52:** Paul connects the Second Coming to the transformation of the believer's body: *"Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed—in a flash, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed."*

### 3. Judgment and Justice
The Second Coming is not only a time of rescue for believers but also a time of reckoning and justice for those who have rejected God and persecuted His people.

*   **2 Thessalonians 1:6-10:** *"God is just: He will pay back trouble to those who trouble you and give relief to you who are troubled... This will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in blazing fire with his powerful angels. He will punish those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus."*
*   **Matthew 25:31-46 (The Sheep and the Goats):** Jesus describes His return as a King sitting on a glorious throne, separating the nations like a shepherd separates sheep from goats, rendering final judgment based on their response to Him and how they treated "the least of these."
*   **Jude 14-15:** Quoting the ancient prophecy of Enoch, Jude writes, *"See, the Lord is coming with thousands upon thousands of his holy ones to judge everyone, and to convict all of them of all the ungodly acts they have committed."*
